Air mismatch: KC throw by design into a DEN secondary giving up 226 pass yds/game. Rashee Rice is the focal point of the attack.

The KC host the DEN as favorites of 2.5, with the total set at 42.5 — a market that implies a KC 22–20 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 26% of its snaps with KC in front, 39% within one score, and 34% with KC chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This is a coin-flip script. With only 2.5 points separating them, neither team projects to spend much time in a blowout state — most of the game lives in the 'close' bucket, where play-calling stays balanced and usage tracks each player's established role rather than being distorted by score. In tight games the stars on both sides see their normal, dependable workloads, and there is less garbage-time leakage to backups.

The Key Matchups

Tough sledding for Kenneth Walker III — DEN are stingy against the run (102 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Patrick Mahomes adds rushing value — he scrambles on 4.8% of dropbacks, live for rush-yard and anytime-TD props.

Tough sledding for J.K. Dobbins — KC are stingy against the run (108 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Courtland Sutton faces a tough cover — KC hold WR1s to just 50 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Touchdown Board

In the red zone KC throw it (56% pass inside the 20) — Rashee Rice's TD equity over a goal-line back.

KC — a pass-heavy offense

KC stay aggressive through the air even with a lead — they pass 50% on early downs when ahead versus the league's 44%. They don't sit on the ball, which keeps their receivers live in scripts where most offenses would be running out the clock.

Kenneth Walker III (15 carries, 65 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Rashee Rice projects for 9 targets and 76 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Travis Kelce (TE, 6 targets, 51 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

DEN — a balanced offense

DEN are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (43% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

J.K. Dobbins (13 carries, 63 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Courtland Sutton projects for 6 targets and 49 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Evan Engram (TE, 3 targets, 21 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 2-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
